noteBlocks.text: Measuring the rate of a reaction

noteBlocks.md: Two lumps of chalk dropped into the same acid fizz for very different lengths of time if one of them has been crushed. Rate is simply how fast the change happens, and the whole of this topic is about measuring that speed and reading it off a graph.

noteBlocks.text: 1. Rate is a change divided by a time

noteBlocks.md:
A **rate** tells you how much something changes in each second. So you measure **how much** the reaction has done and **how long** it took, and divide:
**rate = change ÷ time**.
The change can be a volume of gas made, in cm³, or a mass lost, in g. The unit of the rate follows straight from that: cm³/s or g/s.

noteBlocks.title: Why the flask gets lighter
noteBlocks.md: Nothing is destroyed. The carbon dioxide made in the flask escapes through the cotton wool into the room, and the mass it takes with it is the mass the balance stops seeing. That is why the loss in mass measures how much reaction has happened.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the balance experiment shown, 3.60 g of gas had escaped after 200 s. Work out the mean rate in g/s, to three decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: 3.60 ÷ 200 = 0.018 g/s. Change first, time second, and the unit is the change's unit over seconds.

noteBlocks.text: 2. Three ways to follow the same reaction

noteBlocks.md: CCEA limits you to three methods. **Collect the gas** in a gas syringe and read its volume. **Weigh the flask** and watch the mass fall. Or, where a **precipitate** forms, time how long the mixture takes to turn cloudy enough to hide a cross printed underneath. For the cross there is no volume and no mass, so the rate is written **rate = 1 ÷ time**, in s⁻¹.

noteBlocks.explain: 1 ÷ 32 = 0.031 s⁻¹. A longer time means a smaller rate, which is the whole point of writing it upside down.

noteBlocks.caption: Steep at the start, flat at the end: the two places questions always ask about.

noteBlocks.md: Plot volume against time and the curve tells you three things. Its **steepness** is the rate, so the reaction is fastest at the **start**. Where it **goes flat** the reaction has stopped, because a reactant has run out: here that is at 50 s. And the **height** of that flat stretch is the **total** volume made, 54 cm³ — read it off the plateau, never by adding up the table.

noteBlocks.title: Where this mark goes
noteBlocks.md: In Summer 2025's Chemistry Booklet B a sizeable number **added every volume in the table together** instead of reading the total off the flat stretch. The syringe reading is already a running total, so the last one is the whole amount.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the volume-against-time curve above, the line runs flat from 50 s onwards. What total volume of gas was made, in cm³?
noteBlocks.explain: 54 cm³, the height of the flat stretch. Summer 2025's Booklet B report records a sizeable number of candidates adding every volume in the table instead, which gives a far larger nonsense figure.

noteBlocks.md:
**The question.** Use the graph to calculate the mean rate of reaction between 20 s and 40 s. Give your answer in cm³/s.
**Step 1 — read both volumes, not one.** At 20 s the syringe holds 36 cm³; at 40 s it holds 52 cm³.
**Step 2 — take the change.** 52 − 36 = 16 cm³. This is the step the dashed lines draw.

noteBlocks.prompt: Finish step 2 for the same curve: the volume rises from 36 cm³ at 20 s to 52 cm³ at 40 s. What is the change in volume, in cm³?
noteBlocks.explain: 52 − 36 = 16 cm³. Subtracting is the step that most answers skip, and reading 52 straight off the axis is the commonest wrong route.

noteBlocks.md:
**Step 3 — divide by the time taken.** The time is 40 − 20 = 20 s, not 40 s.
**Step 4 — divide and keep the unit.** 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8 cm³/s.
Compare it with the very start, where the curve climbs 22 cm³ in the first 10 s: a rate of 2.2 cm³/s. The reaction really has slowed down, because the acid is being used up.

noteBlocks.prompt: Use the same rule on the whole reaction: 54 cm³ of gas was collected and the curve went flat at 50 s. Give the mean rate in cm³/s, to two decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08 cm³/s. Divide by the time the reaction actually took, not by the last time printed in the table.

steps.working: Follow the curve to the right until it stops rising. It runs flat at 54 cm³, so the total volume of gas is 54 cm³.
steps.decision: Read the total off the flat part of the curve. Adding the volumes in the table counts the same gas over and over, and Summer 2025's report names it as a real error.

options: Because the syringe reading is a running total already, so the last one is the whole lot
Because each reading is the gas made since the last reading
Because the table stops before the reaction does
whyMenu.explain: The syringe never empties, so every reading includes all the gas made so far. The final reading is the total.

steps.working: The curve becomes flat at 50 s, so the reaction finished at 50 s.
steps.decision: Flat means nothing more is happening. The table runs on to 60 s, but the reaction was over before that.

steps.working: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken
steps.decision: Write the rule before the numbers. The rule is what tells you which number goes on top.
Substitute the time the reaction took, 50 s, not the last time in the table. Dividing by 60 s gives 0.9 cm³/s and loses the answer mark.
Two decimal places because the question said so, and the unit is the volume unit over seconds.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 54 cm³. (b) 50 s. (c) rate = change ÷ time = 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08 cm³/s.

steps.working: Changed (independent): the size of the calcium carbonate pieces — large chips, small chips, powder.
steps.decision: The independent variable is the one you deliberately alter. Name the sizes, because 'surface area' on its own does not say what you would put in the flask.

steps.working: Measured (dependent): the volume of carbon dioxide collected in the gas syringe at fixed times.
steps.decision: Say what is measured and in what, not just 'the rate'. The rate is worked out afterwards; the syringe reading is what you record.

steps.working: Kept the same: the mass of calcium carbonate, and the volume and concentration of the acid. The temperature of the acid too.
steps.decision: A control variable is one that would change the rate if you let it. Naming the same variable twice in different words earns one mark, not two.

options: Because only then can a difference in rate be blamed on the surface area
Because the experiment would be unsafe otherwise
Because the gas syringe only works at one temperature
whyMenu.explain: Control variables are what make the comparison fair: change one thing and hold the rest still, or you cannot say what caused the difference.

steps.working: A table with time / s in the first column and volume of gas / cm³ in the second, one row every 10 s, and one table for each size of chip.
steps.decision: Column headings carry the unit. Summer 2025's Booklet B report records the missing axis unit as the commonest lost mark, and the table headings are where the axis labels come from.

(c) In a results table with the headings time / s and volume of gas / cm³, a reading every 10 s, one table per size.

items.stem: Which of these is a unit of volume?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — reading units; you are not expected to have met rates yet

options.feedback: Cubic centimetres. Every gas-syringe reading in this lesson is in cm³.
Grams measure mass. Both turn up in this topic, so it is worth separating them before you start.
Seconds measure time. The rate unit puts a volume over a time, so you need to be able to tell them apart.

items.stem: A car travels 90 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
items.skill: Prerequisite from mathematics — a rate is an amount divided by a time

options.feedback: 90 ÷ 3 = 30. Every rate in chemistry is built the same way: the change divided by the time.
That multiplies. A rate divides the amount by the time, so 90 ÷ 3 = 30 km/h.
That is the time divided by the distance, which is the fraction upside down. Section 1 of the lesson is about which number goes on top.

items.stem: Marble chips are calcium carbonate. Which gas is given off when they react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.8 — reactions of acids with carbonates

options.feedback: Acid plus a carbonate always gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide. That gas is what every method in this lesson is following.
Hydrogen comes from an acid with a metal. With a carbonate the gas is carbon dioxide, and limewater turning milky is the test.
Oxygen comes from hydrogen peroxide with a catalyst, which is one of the other reactions on this specification. A carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

items.stem: A gas syringe reads 0, 22, 36, 46, 52, 54 and 54 cm³ at 10 s intervals. What total volume of gas was produced?
items.skill: Read a total from a set of syringe readings

options.feedback: The readings are a running total, so the last one is the whole amount. On a graph it is the height of the flat stretch.
That adds every reading together, counting the same gas six times over. Summer 2025's Booklet B report names this exact error.
That is the gas made after the first 20 s only. The total is everything collected from the start.
That is the reading after 10 s, not the total. Follow the readings to the end, where they stop changing.

items.stem: A reaction produces 54 cm³ of gas and the curve goes flat at 50 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.feedback: 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08. Volume on top, time underneath, unit cm³/s.
That is the time divided by the volume, the fraction upside down. Rate is always the change on top.
That divides by the last time printed in the table. The reaction was over before then, so use the time it actually took.
That multiplies instead of dividing. A rate is an amount per second, so the time goes underneath.

items.stem: Which apparatus would you use to measure the volume of carbon dioxide given off in a reaction?
items.skill: Name the apparatus for a method

options.feedback: A gas syringe, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water. Keep the word gas: 'syringe' alone lost marks in Summer 2025.
The balance follows the mass lost, which is the other method. It never tells you a volume.
A thermometer is for the temperature-change experiments in the energy topic, not for measuring a gas.
The reaction happens in the conical flask, but the flask does not measure anything. The gas syringe does.

items.stem: In the disappearing-cross experiment the cross was hidden after 32 s. Using rate = 1 ÷ time, what is the rate?

options.feedback: 1 ÷ 32 = 0.031 s⁻¹. A longer time gives a smaller rate, which is what you want it to do.
That is the time itself, not one divided by it. The rule turns the time upside down on purpose.
That turns the time into minutes first, so the answer is per minute. The unit asked for is s⁻¹, so keep the time in seconds.
The number is right but the unit is not. One divided by a time in seconds gives a rate per second, written s⁻¹, and CCEA marks that unit separately.

items.stem: A reaction between 2.0 g of marble chips and excess acid gives 54 cm³ of gas. It is repeated with the same 2.0 g crushed to a powder. What does the new curve do?
items.skill: Sketch the effect of a change on a rate curve

options.text: it is steeper and levels off at 54 cm³
options.feedback: Steeper because it is faster, and the same height because the same mass of carbonate can only make the same amount of gas.

options.text: it is steeper and levels off above 54 cm³
options.feedback: A faster reaction makes the same gas sooner, not more of it. Summer 2025 recorded 2 of 3 marks on exactly this sketch because the line did not level off at the original value.

options.text: it is less steep and levels off at 54 cm³
options.feedback: Powder has a much larger surface area, so the reaction is faster and the curve is steeper, not shallower.

options.text: it is steeper and never levels off
options.feedback: Every curve levels off once a reactant runs out. With 2.0 g of carbonate that happens at the same height as before.

items.stem: A results table has the headings 'Time' and 'Volume of gas'. What is missing?

options.feedback: Units belong in the heading, and the axis labels are copied straight from there. The missing x-axis label was the commonest lost mark in Summer 2025's Booklet B.
The rate is worked out afterwards from the readings; it is not something you record at the bench. The units are what the headings are missing.
A heading without a unit does not say what the numbers are. Write 'Time / s' and 'Volume of gas / cm³'.
A title is never a mark. The unit in each heading is.

figures.alt: A curve of the volume of carbon dioxide against time: steep at the start, bending over and running flat from fifty seconds onwards.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the volume of carbon dioxide collected when marble chips reacted with dilute hydrochloric acid.
Use the graph to find the total volume of gas produced.

scheme.for: 54 (cm³), read from the flat part of the curve
scheme.examinerNote: Adding the readings in the table is not credited; the syringe reading is already a running total.

hints: Follow the curve right until it stops rising.
The syringe is never emptied, so each reading includes all the gas so far.
parts.workedSolution: The curve stops rising at 50 s and runs flat at 54 cm³, so the total volume of gas is 54 cm³.

commonErrors.feedback: That is every reading in the table added together, which counts the same gas over and over. The syringe reading is a running total, so the answer is the last one, 54 cm³.

figures.alt: A curve of the volume of carbon dioxide against time: steep at the start, bending over and running flat from fifty seconds onwards.

parts.stem:
The curve levels off at 50 s, by which time 54 cm³ of carbon dioxide had been collected.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction. Give your answer in cm³/s to two decimal places.

scheme.for: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken (in words or symbols)

scheme.examinerNote: The decimal-place instruction is a mark in its own right; an unrounded answer loses it.

hints: Write the rule before the numbers.
The reaction was over at 50 s, so that is the time it took.
parts.workedSolution: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken = 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08 cm³/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by 60 s, the last time printed in the table. The reaction had already finished, so divide by 50 s.
That is the time divided by the volume. Rate always has the change on top, so the unit comes out as cm³/s rather than s/cm³.

parts.stem:
On the curve the volume of gas is 36 cm³ at 20 s and 52 cm³ at 40 s.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction between 20 s and 40 s, in cm³/s.

scheme.for: divides by the time taken, 40 − 20 = 20 s

hints: Two readings, so the volume you want is the difference between them.
The time is the gap between the two times, not the later one.
parts.workedSolution: change in volume = 52 − 36 = 16 cm³; time taken = 40 − 20 = 20 s; rate = 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8 cm³/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the total volume at 40 s, 52 cm³, instead of the change. Take the reading at 20 s away first: 52 − 36 = 16 cm³.
That is the gradient of the first stretch of the curve, from 0 to 20 s. The question names a different section, and the curve is much less steep there.
That is the time divided by the change in volume. The change goes on top, so the unit reads cm³ per second.

parts.stem:
Use the completed table. The reading stopped falling after 200 s.
Calculate the mean rate of reaction in g/s. Give your answer to three decimal places.

scheme.for: rate = loss in mass ÷ time taken

hints: The change is the loss in mass, not the balance reading.

parts.workedSolution: rate = loss in mass ÷ time taken = 3.60 ÷ 200 = 0.018 g/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the final balance reading instead of the mass lost. The flask and its contents were never the change; the change is 96.80 − 93.20 = 3.60 g.

parts.stem:
Over the first 10 s the curve is almost a straight line from the origin, reaching 22 cm³ at 10 s.
Calculate the gradient of that first stretch, in cm³/s. This is the rate of reaction at the start.

scheme.examinerNote: The unit of a gradient is the y-axis unit over the x-axis unit; Summer 2025 Booklet B records the gradient unit as poorly known.

hints: Rise is the change up the axis, run is the change across.
That stretch starts at the origin, so the rise is the whole reading.
parts.workedSolution: gradient = rise ÷ run = 22 ÷ 10 = 2.2 cm³/s, which is the rate of reaction at the start.

commonErrors.feedback: That is run over rise, the gradient upside down. Rise goes on top, so the unit comes out as cm³ per second rather than seconds per cm³.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the volume of carbon dioxide collected when 2.0 g of marble chips reacted with 40 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid.
Use the graph to find the time at which the reaction finished.
hints: The reaction stops where the curve stops climbing.
parts.workedSolution: The curve is flat from 50 s onwards, so the reaction finished at 50 s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is where the table stops, not where the reaction stopped. The last change in volume happened at 50 s.

parts.stem: Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the whole reaction. Give your answer in cm³/s to two decimal places.

scheme.for: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken

hints: Use your answer to part (a) as the time.

commonErrors.feedback: That starts from the sum of every reading in the table. The total volume is the plateau, 54 cm³, so the rate is 1.08 cm³/s.

parts.stem:
The experiment was repeated with the same mass of marble chips crushed to a powder, and the same volume and concentration of acid.
Describe the curve that would be obtained.

accepted: the curve is steeper at the start and levels off at the same volume of gas
it rises more steeply and finishes at the same height as before

scheme.for: steeper at the start (the reaction is faster)
levels off at the same volume of gas as the original curve
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 records most candidates scoring 2 of 3 on this sketch because the line did not level off at the original value.

hints: Think about the mass of carbonate: it has not changed.
Two things to say: how steep, and where it finishes.
parts.workedSolution: The curve is steeper at the start because the powder reacts faster, and it levels off at the same volume of gas, because the same mass of calcium carbonate can only make the same amount of carbon dioxide.

pattern.regex: \bhigher volume\b|\bmore gas\b|\bgreater volume\b|\bfinishes higher\b|\bhigher than the original\b|\bmore carbon dioxide\b

commonErrors.feedback: A faster reaction makes the same gas sooner, not more of it. The mass of calcium carbonate fixes the finishing height, so the new curve levels off at the same place.

parts.stem: Suggest one other method that could have been used to follow the same reaction, and say what would be measured.

accepted: weigh the flask on a balance and measure the loss in mass
put the flask on a top-pan balance and record the mass lost

scheme.for: stand the flask on a (top-pan) balance
measure the loss in mass (in g) against time
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2023 records 'amount' written in place of mass or grams as the commonest loss here.

hints: The gas leaves the flask, so something else changes as well as the volume collected.
parts.workedSolution: Stand the conical flask on a top-pan balance with cotton wool in its neck and record the loss in mass at fixed times as the carbon dioxide escapes.

commonErrors.feedback: Say what you would actually read: the loss in mass, in grams. 'Amount' is the word Summer 2023 examiners named as the reason this mark was lost.

parts.stem:
Describe how you would investigate whether powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than the same mass of large chips.
In your answer name the apparatus, say what you would measure and how often, and say what you would keep the same.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: Name the apparatus: a conical flask closed with a bung and delivery tube, leading to a gas syringe.
Use the same mass of calcium carbonate each time, for example 2.0 g.
Use the same volume and the same concentration of hydrochloric acid each time.
Start the stopwatch as the acid and the carbonate meet.
Record the volume of gas in the syringe at fixed times, for example every 10 s.
Repeat the whole run with the powder, keeping everything else the same.
Plot volume of gas against time for both runs and compare how steep the curves are.

scheme.for: a banded description of the method: apparatus named, the variable changed, the variable measured and how often, the variables held constant, and how the two runs are compared
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Name the apparatus in full, and say how often you would read it.
Say what you keep the same, and why that makes the comparison fair.
parts.workedSolution: Weigh out 2.0 g of large calcium carbonate chips and put them in a conical flask. Add 40 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid, close the flask with a bung and delivery tube leading to a gas syringe, and start the stopwatch at once. Record the volume of gas in the syringe every 10 s until it stops changing. Repeat the whole run with 2.0 g of powdered calcium carbonate and the same volume and concentration of acid. Plot volume of gas against time for both runs: the steeper curve is the faster reaction, and both should level off at the same volume.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'The table shows the volume of carbon dioxide collected every 10 s. Use it to find the total volume of gas and the mean rate of reaction in cm³/s. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: The readings stop changing at 50 s, so the reaction took 50 s.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The gas syringe is never emptied, so each reading already contains all the gas collected so far. Adding the column counts the same gas seven times over. The total is the last reading, 54 cm³, which is the height of the flat stretch on the graph.
correction: Total volume = 54 cm³ (the final reading, where the curve goes flat)
findTheMistake.feedback: The finishing time is right and the rule is right, so two of the three marks stand. Only the total goes: a syringe reading is a running total, so the answer is the last one, 54 cm³, and the rate becomes 1.08 cm³/s. Summer 2025's Booklet B report records this exact addition.

prompts.prompt: Write the rule for the rate of a reaction measured as a gas volume, and give its unit.
prompts.answer: rate = change in volume ÷ time taken, in cm³/s.

prompts.prompt: A reaction is followed by timing how long a printed cross takes to be hidden. What is the rule for the rate, and its unit?
Name the three ways CCEA allows you to follow the rate of a reaction.
prompts.answer: Measure the change in mass on a balance, measure the volume of gas collected, or time how long a precipitate takes to form.

prompts.prompt: A gas syringe is read every 10 s. How do you find the total volume of gas produced?
prompts.answer: Take the last reading, where the readings stop changing: on the graph it is the height of the flat stretch. Do not add the readings together, because each one is a running total.

prompts.prompt: On a volume-against-time curve, what does the steepness tell you, and what does the flat part tell you?
prompts.answer: The steepness is the rate, so the reaction is fastest at the start. The flat part means the reaction has stopped because a reactant has been used up.

prompts.prompt: The same mass of carbonate is used but the chips are crushed. Where does the new curve finish, and why?
prompts.answer: At the same height as the original curve, because the same mass of carbonate can only make the same amount of gas. It just gets there sooner.

prompts.prompt: Name the two pieces of apparatus in the gas-collection method, in the words the mark scheme wants.
prompts.answer: A gas syringe measures the volume of gas, and the reaction takes place in a conical flask.

prompts.prompt: What must every column heading of a results table carry, and what does that decide on the graph?
prompts.answer: Its unit, written as Time / s or Volume of gas / cm³. The axis labels are copied straight from the headings, and a missing axis unit is the commonest lost mark.

findings.asked: Plot gas volume against time for marble chips in acid, read the total volume and the finishing time, sketch the curve for powder, and draw the apparatus.
findings.wentWrong: The missing x-axis label was the commonest single loss. A sizeable number added every volume in the table instead of reading the plateau. Apparatus drawings were mostly good but must be flat, in section, with no line across a tube or stopper, and 'gas' was dropped from 'gas syringe'.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Labelled both axes with their units, plotted every point, drew one smooth curve, read the total off the flat stretch, and drew an open path from the flask to the syringe.
findings.rule: The total is the height of the plateau; the reaction ends where the curve goes flat.

findings.asked: Calculate the rate of the fastest reaction to three decimal places, then sketch the curve for half the concentration.
findings.wentWrong: The arithmetic was usually right; the three-decimal-place instruction was what lost the mark, and some worked out all four rates when one was asked for. The sketch scored 2 of 3 because it did not level off at the original final mass.
findings.rule: The same amount of the limiting reactant gives the same finishing value; a slower run is a shallower curve to the same height.

findings.asked: Identify the apparatus used to measure a rate, then describe how the rate was measured.
findings.wentWrong: Few named the apparatus, and 'amount' written in place of mass or grams lost the marks for the method.
findings.rule: Say what you measure (mass in grams, volume in cm³) and over what time.

insight.ruleToRemember: Rate = change ÷ time, with the unit the change came in; rate = 1 ÷ time for a disappearing cross. On a graph the steepness is the rate, the flat part is the finish, and the height of the flat part is the total. Read totals from the plateau, put units in every heading and axis label, and draw apparatus flat and open.
insight.aStarSignal: Sketching a changed run with the right steepness AND the right finishing height, and saying why the finishing height cannot change.
